title: Graph isomorphism in BQP
formal: Does the ordinary graph-isomorphism decision problem belong to \(\mathrm{BQP}\), bounded-error quantum polynomial time? That is, do there exist one uniform quantum algorithm and integers \(C,c\ge1\) such that, for every pair of finite simple graphs given by their complete binary adjacency matrices, the algorithm decides whether a vertex bijection preserves adjacency, with error at most \(1/3\), using at most \(C(n+2)^c\) total elementary operations, where \(n\) is the larger vertex count? No distributional or structural promise is imposed on the graphs.
definitions:
For an integer \(r\ge0\), write \([r]=\{1,\ldots,r\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A finite simple graph on \([r]\) is an undirected graph with no loops or parallel edges. Its adjacency matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{r\times r}\) is symmetric with zero diagonal. Each input graph is encoded by its binary order with a self-delimiting length prefix, followed by all adjacency entries in row-major order; the two graph encodings are concatenated. A prefix can be encoded as \(1^t0\) followed by a \(t\)-bit binary order, using \(t\ge1\) and the usual minimal binary representation. Invalid encodings are rejected. Graphs of different orders are not isomorphic. If both have order \(r\), an isomorphism is a bijection \(\pi:[r]\to[r]\) such that \[A_{uv}=B_{\pi(u),\pi(v)}\qquad\text{for every }u,v\in[r].\] The two order-zero graphs are isomorphic. A yes-instance has at least one such bijection; a no-instance has none. The algorithm must accept every yes-instance with probability at least \(2/3\) and every no-instance with probability at most \(1/3\). Its probability is over its quantum measurement outcomes and any internal random bits, separately for each fixed input. It receives only the explicit classical input, with no witness, nonuniform advice, graph-orbit state, isomorphism oracle, promised rigidity, degree bound or typical-input assumption. Here GI denotes this ordinary permutation-based relation, not the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism in nonlocal-game theory. The running time is polynomial in the graph order and hence in the explicit input length; malformed encodings must be rejected in time polynomial in their actual length.

The allowed elementary gates are \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), where \[H=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle.\] Here \(a,b\) are bits and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. A quantum register of \(r\) qubits has computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^r\}\); its pure state is a unit vector \(\sum_z\alpha_z|z\rangle\) with complex coefficients. Gates act by their specified unitary matrices on selected qubits and as identity elsewhere. A computational-basis measurement of a register has outcome probabilities given by the squared norms of its corresponding state components. All working qubits start at zero. Classical control is performed by one finite Turing program with no advice; each classical bit step, each elementary gate, and each measured or initialized qubit is charged. Fair random bits, if used, cost one step each. All executions halt within the displayed worst-case bound. This uniform circuit-and-control model charges total work, including input parsing, data preparation, classical postprocessing and output, rather than only circuit depth.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified language lies in BQP, including uniformity, bounded error on every input and polynomial total work, or a complete Lean-checked proof that it does not lie in BQP. A classical polynomial-time algorithm is a valid affirmative solution because it can be implemented within the quantum model with polynomial overhead. A negative proof must exclude all uniform bounded-error polynomial-time quantum algorithms, rather than only coset-state, Fourier-sampling or photonic-sampling methods. A necessary invariant that distinguishes only some nonisomorphic graphs, an efficient fixed relaxation, or uncharged preparation of a helpful state does not establish membership. The output is a proof of the yes/no complexity statement, not an approximate isomorphism score.
why: A canonical test of whether quantum computation can efficiently recognize equivalence of explicit combinatorial structures, beyond the algebraic problems already handled by standard period finding.

importance.reason: A central quantum-algorithm target linking graph algorithms, permutation groups and the computational use of entangled states.

progress.text: Aaronson lists graph isomorphism as a target for new quantum algorithmic ideas.
Coset-state lower bounds establish the need for highly joint measurements in the standard hidden-subgroup approach; the joint journal paper appears in 2010.
Babai gives a classical quasipolynomial-time algorithm; his January 2017 update repairs the affected recursion and restores the bound.
Kar–Roberson–Seppelt–Zeman publish polynomial algorithms for fixed levels of a hierarchy for a different quantum isomorphism relation.
Gheorghiu and coauthors classify several group-action quantum state problems, with GI-hardness for the Clifford-group version.
Maxwell–van den Hoven–Renema revise their quantum-inspired necessary-condition algorithm; its sufficient full-order version is not efficient.

context_blocks.text: Graph isomorphism asks whether two descriptions encode the same finite relational structure after renaming the vertices. It is an exact equivalence problem, rather than a search for approximately similar networks. A proposed permutation is easy to verify by comparing all adjacency entries, but finding a successful permutation or ruling out every permutation can require reasoning about highly symmetric graphs.

Elementary invariants help without settling the problem. For instance, a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices, six edges and degree two at every vertex, but cannot be isomorphic because one is connected and the other is not. More elaborate invariants must likewise be assessed by whether they distinguish every required pair, not just by how well they perform on a test set.

Aaronson’s 2005 challenge list identifies graph isomorphism among the natural targets for quantum algorithms beyond Shor and Grover. The formulation on this card turns that broad research motivation into one exact complexity-class membership question. It imposes no particular algorithmic approach and permits a classical algorithm as a special case of a quantum one.

Babai’s classical breakthrough gives a quasipolynomial-time algorithm, with bound \(\exp ((\log  n)^{O(1)})\). The original argument required a correction in January 2017, after which the quasipolynomial claim was restored. This is the relevant general classical benchmark, rather than brute-force examination of n! permutations. Quasipolynomial time is still larger than the polynomial bound asked for here.

A classical adjacency matrix is the entire input resource. Preparing a special quantum representation of its relabelings is additional computation and must be charged. Distinguishability of hypothetical states therefore cannot substitute for a complete uniform algorithm that prepares and processes its data within the required running time.

The established hidden-subgroup approach makes this difficulty precise in another form. Graph isomorphism can be reduced to finding hidden symmetry in permutation groups, and the standard procedure generates quantum coset states. Hallgren, Roetteler and Sen, independently of Moore and Russell and later in joint work, prove that measurements on too few such states reveal insufficient information in the relevant hard cases. Their bound requires joint access to \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) states to obtain useful information.

That lower bound is a restriction on information extraction in a particular representation. The number of required states is itself polynomial. It does not say that every measurement on that many states needs superpolynomial computation, and it does not forbid an algorithm that uses the explicit input graphs in a different way. A negative solution to \(GI\in \mathrm{BQP}\) would have to rule out those broader possibilities as well.

The inherited quantum-inspired reference has a substantive June 2026 revision. Maxwell, van den Hoven and Renema analyze correlations in Gaussian boson samplers and derive a classical test for a necessary condition of graph isomorphism. At restricted correlation order it can certify that some graph pairs are different. At the maximum order their condition becomes sufficient, but their method is no longer efficient. The authors explicitly separate these two regimes.

This illustrates why a photonic sampling procedure is not automatically a polynomial-time decision algorithm for all graphs. One must account for how many samples or correlations are required to distinguish a worst-case pair, how accurately they must be estimated, and the classical work used to interpret them. Efficiently generating individual samples does not by itself establish a uniform bound for the complete decision task.

May 2026 work by Gheorghiu, Jacobs, Mehraban and Motamedi studies isomorphism of quantum states under group actions. They show, among other results, that a Clifford-group state problem is at least as hard as ordinary graph isomorphism, while a Pauli-group variant is BQP-complete. The direction and the group matter: the BQP algorithm for the Pauli problem is not thereby an algorithm for the GI-hard Clifford problem.

The 2026 paper by Kar, Roberson, Seppelt and Zeman concerns the different relation called quantum graph isomorphism. It gives randomized polynomial-time algorithms for exact feasibility at each fixed level of a hierarchy of noncommutative semidefinite relaxations. Neither the relation nor a fixed relaxation is the ordinary vertex-bijection decision problem posed here.

A positive answer would enlarge the collection of important exact structure problems known to admit efficient quantum algorithms, unless a classical polynomial algorithm arrived at the same time. A negative answer would be exceptionally strong: GI has efficiently verifiable permutation witnesses and hence belongs to NP, so \(GI\notin \mathrm{BQP}\) would in particular imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The question is fundamental on both sides, independently of any particular physical implementation.

sentences: Two graphs are isomorphic when a relabeling of vertices preserves every edge.
This question asks whether a quantum algorithm can decide that equivalence in polynomial time for every pair of explicitly given graphs.
The algorithm must include all processing costs and achieve bounded error, rather than merely extract a small amount of information from an oracle.
Symmetry makes graph isomorphism a natural testing ground for quantum methods, but quantum access to related group structure is not itself a complete algorithm.
A resolution would clarify whether quantum computation can efficiently handle this central classification problem.
